articles.text:
We have remaining a few sets of Huffmann's instantaneous round-up views, representing the most interesting events of the range cattle industry. articles.headline: ELECTION! Reports from Various Sources.
articles.text:
BISMARCK, Nov. 3.—Gifford is elected by a majority estimated at not over twenty-five thousand. The entire republican ticket in Burleigh county, with the exception of Neal for sheriff. Frank Donnelly beat him for the office. On the legislative ticket, Hughes and Williams, republican, have majorities of 1,000 to 1,500 and Greene, democrat, has majority of 500 over Steele.

MANDAN, Nov. 4.—Greene has a majority over Steele of about 700 in the district.

ST. PAUL, MINN., Nov. 4.—McGill's majority as republican candidate for governor is about 5,000.

MILES CCTY, MONT., Nov. 4—The Democrats elected Toole as delegate by about 1,5000 majority. The vote was remarkably close.

GLENDIVE, MONT., Nov. 3—Tuttle defeated Matthews for sheriff by a small majority.

DICKINSON, DAK., Nov. 3.—There was never more scratching done here than at this election. Complete returns are not in but candidates were elected on all the tickets. Sebastian is defeated for Sheriff.
articles.summary: Election returns from Bismarck, Mandan, St. Paul, Miles City, Glendive and Dickinson: Gifford elected delegate, Hughes, Williams and Greene elected to the legislature, Toole elected Montana delegate.

articles.text: It will be remembered that at the last meetings of the National Cattle Growers' Association and the National Cattle and Horse Growers' Association, committees were appointed from each to arrange for a union of the two associations. This union was accomplished under the title of Consolidated Cattle Growers' Association of the United States and the next meeting will be held in Chicago, Nov. 16 and 17. It seems that now is the accepted time for every cattle association to represent at this convention and together, as one man, adopt measures that will finally and forever stamp out pleuro-pneumonia from the soil of the United States. Time is too precious now to indulge in factional or sectional fights. The battle against pleuro-pneumonia and other diseases can best be waged through the medium of the Consolidated association. Each association, if working by itself, can accomplish little or nothing. All should unite in the larger association and protect themselves and their neighbors from the imminent danger of contagious diseases on the range.
articles.summary: Urges every cattle association to be represented at the Consolidated Cattle Growers' Association meeting in Chicago, Nov. 16-17, to fight pleuro-pneumonia.

articles.text: The St. Paul stock-yards scheme is having another boom by the formation of a company with a capital of $1,500,000 for the purpose of erecting immense feed stables, slaughtering and packing houses to utilize as much as possible of the range product of the northwest. This move is closely watched by stockmen of this country and a long sigh of relief will go up from them as soon as the yards are in successful operation.
articles.summary: A $1,500,000 company is being formed to build feed stables and packing houses at the St. Paul stock-yards for northwestern range cattle.

articles.text: The Miles City Dressed Beef Co's slaughter-house was closed last week by the action of numerous creditors levying attachments on the works. The outstanding accounts in Montana aggregate about $95,000 and the backer of the concern, L. M. Dustin of Lincoln, Ill., is a financial wreck. His bank at Lincoln is also closed, owing to a run on it. In what ever light this matter is placed it cannot but be a misforture to the range country. There is no denying the fact that cowmen are being underpaid for their live beef and large slaughter-houses in the range country are one of the feelers put out to find a good road for the cattlemen out of present "slough of dispond" of low prices. As far as the feeler in Miles City is concerned, it did not live long enough to prove anything besides the incompetence of the management. It is to be hoped that some practical ranchmen can form a partnership with a practical butcher, to thoroughly test the matter of slaughtering beef on the range for the wholesale trade. Should the attempt prove unsuccessful, there seems no other way than that rangemen should pool together to raise prices or to adopt the Medora plan of killing on the range and retailing in large cities.
articles.summary: The Miles City Dressed Beef Co.'s slaughter-house was closed by creditors; the paper urges ranchmen to test range slaughtering or adopt the Medora plan.

articles.text: Six thousand of Swift & Co's and Nelson Morris' beef butchers struck Monday morning sooner than return to the ten-hour-a-day rule. Two or three hundred canners from Libby, McNeal & Libby also struck as their firm was getting beef from the above firms. This will undoubtedly be the last stand made in Chicago against working ten hours a day. If all employes in the United States of any one trade should work eight hours a day, there would probably be no trouble except for the fact of machinery and capital lying idle a fifth longer than was expected when the works were erected. This difficulty could doubtless be remedied, but that of one or more firms working on the eight-hour plan with ten hours' pay while all other firms work ten hours places the first at a disadvantage that will soon find the bottom of the best-filled pocket. It is simply a financial impossibility for a firm in any business to pay twenty per cent. more for their employes than do other firms. Since last May, this is exactly what the Chicago packers have been doing and they now find that they must either stop it or close up their works. If the butchers all over the United States were well enough organized to all demand eight hours' work, the plan would be successful and after things were adjusted to the new order, entirely satisfactory. Until the butchers are so organized, however, it is folly to ask any one employer or the employers in any one town to adopt a plan that places them at such a disadvantage that a proffitable business is impossible.
articles.summary: Comment on the strike of 6,000 Chicago packing-house butchers against the return to the ten-hour day.

articles.headline: Ear Marks.
articles.text:
A cattleman remarked the other day in our presence that "bad ear marks make bad cattle." In answer to the inquiry why? he said he did not know, but that he had observed in handling range cattle that animals with their ears gone or badly disfigured were ugly and difficulty to drive.

The remark caused us to philosophise as follows. The ears were given to animals for a certain purpose and the law of adaptation was faithfully carried out in the matter of construction. Without going into the details of the formation of the bovine ear it is sufficient to say that it is so shaped as to catch the slightest vibration of sound and lead it directly to the organs of intelligence or instinct, as the reader may see proper to class that intellectual power our dumb animals process. The cutting off the ear destroys the natural conduit of sound and throws it upon the inner organs with such violence as to produce an abnormal effect and very rapidly destroy them. So to, does the carving of the ear into many parts by slits, crops or bites destroy the approach of sounds and give exaggerated notions of danger. All this tends to make an animal nervous, and very practical cowmen knows that this means trouble when he attemps move cattle on the range or road. One or two nervous animals in a bunch of beef steers on the way to the shipping point cause a shrinkage in the herd of more than the value of one or even a dozen, in many instances, by stampeding or causing unnecessary excitement.

The ear mark is really of little value, so long as brands are used, in determining the ownership and they might be dispensed with. At least such marks should be used as will effect in the least the hearing of the cattle, and these will be those that do not greatly disfigure the ear.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted argument from the N. W. L. S. Journal that disfiguring ear marks make range cattle nervous and hard to drive.

articles.headline: Cattle Feeding on a College Farm.
articles.text:
CHAMPAIGN, Ill.
Eds. The Farmer:—On October 15, at the regular weighing of cattle on the farm of the [University of?] Illinois, a lot of six choice steers, averaging a few days less than 30 months in age, and 1,603 pounds in weight, were found to have made an average gain of 89 1-9 pounds in 45 days (from September 1) and of 27½ pounds in the last 19 days.

A lot of four good steers, averaging a little over 30 months, and 1,455 pounds had made average gain of 150 pounds in 45 days, and of 58¾ in the 16 days.

A lot of 24 steers of poorer quality and probably of not much less age, averaging 1,118 lbs., had made an average gain of 118½ pounds in the 45 days, and of 44 pounds in the 16 days.

The lot of six have been on a full grain feed during all the summer and last winter—four of them also during the preceding summer. The lot of four were well fed last winter, but had no grain from May 1 until August 15—on full feed since September 1. The lot of 25, with one exception, were purchased in the spring and summer, and had been poorly fed during the winter. Since August 15, they have had same treatment as the lot of four. The average gain of the 24 purchased since June 12, when most of them were bought, has been 242½ pounds.

These cattle have all been on pasture and have been fed on corn in the ear, averaging about one-half bushel per steer daily. They are fed three times a day—generally from the wagon as it comes from the field. The lot of six best steers have not had so good pasture as the others and have eaten a little hay. Pigs "follow" all the cattle and have grown rapidly from the corn left undigested by them. The variations in the rate of grain are partly explainable from the poorer quality and smaller size of the larger lot of steers and from the longer feeding and much higher degree of fatness of the lot of six.

The facts concerning these cattle are in accordance with our experience year after year on the university farm, which seems to show that, under present conditions in Central Illinois:

1. Increase of weight in cattle is most cheaply secured by pasturage without any grain during the best part of the season.

2. Feeding whole corn in the autumn months to cattle on the pasture is the most economical method of fattening cattle. The feeding is done with the least labor. When hogs follow the cattle there is very little waste. The manure is saved and distributed without cost. While comparatively low prices are to be expected for cattle marketed in the autumn or early winter, a fair profit has been made annually. Even with the prevailing exceptionally low prices, sales have been made (for November delivery) of most of the cattle purchased last spring at a price which gives fairly satisfactory profit.

3. After three or four months of full grain feeding a considerable decrease in rate of grain may be expected.

4. Apparently, from 30 to 36 months are the most profitable ages at which to sell cattle fattened on this system—unless those of a little greater age can be bought at a price which gives no profit to the grower.

5. It is not profitable to feed grain to yearling steers on good pasture, if it is designed to keep them another year and fatten for the general market.

6. Calves reared on skim milk, with addition of some meal may make entirely satisfactory growth and beef animals of good quality. A high grade Short-Horn steer now on the farm weighs 1,470 pounds at a few days over 29 months, and with less than two months full grain feeding. He has gained 185 pounds in the last 45 days.

The four steers recently put on grain averaged 153 pounds less than the six which have been kept on full feed—or comparing them with the four of the latter lot of like breeding, and almost exactly the same age, the difference in average weight is 172 pounds. Two steers of the lot of six, which were not grain fed in summer of 1885, lack, the pair, only 115 lbs. of the weight of their mates which were full fed that summer.

Pure bred or grade Ayrshire, Hereford, Holstein and Short-horn cattle, aside from some "common" stock, are in these lots, but not in sufficient number to enable one to dogmatize as to merits of the breeds. The heaviest cattle are half-blood Holsteins. The greatest weight is 1,785 pounds for a steer not quite 31 months old. The steer of best quality is a three-quarter Hereford. A pure bred Ayrshire weighs 1,525 pounds at 32 months. The steer of best form is a pure bred Short-Horn, but a local trouble has reduced his weight 200 pounds or more.

G. E. MORROW,
Prof. of Agriculture.
University, Champaign, Ill.
articles.summary: Letter from Prof. G. E. Morrow reporting feeding results for steers on the University of Illinois farm and conclusions on fattening cattle.

articles.text: The river this fall is even more uncertain than usual. Heavy rains above raised the water higher than it had been since last spring and quicksand was almost as abundant as water. Several teams had trouble in getting out of the treacherous stuff. To-day, it is rapidly lowering and is easily fordable.
articles.summary: Heavy rains upriver raised the Little Missouri to its highest since spring, with quicksand trapping teams; it is now falling and fordable.

articles.text: A special telegram was received from Theodore Roosevelt by the Ferris brothers, that he was defeated in the election for mayor of New York city. There was only remote chance of his election owing to the division in sentiment among the democrats. He made a good fight, ably backed by the best citizens of New York but the anti-reform element was too strong.

articles.text: It seems proper to give an explanation of the defeat of A. T. Packard as justice of the peace. He had absolutely and unqualifiedly refused to run for any office and returned the same answer when urged to run for justice of the peace by Messrs. Willis Eaton and Gregor Lang and many others. He even went so far in his refusal as to say that he would not even run for an office for ten times the combined salaries of all the county officers. Messrs. Eaton and Lang finally put the matter on a basis of pure personal obligation, urging that he was the stockmens' choice and that he should throw aside personal feeling and oblige them to that extent. This was the reason which impelled him to accept a nomination which he not only did not want, but which under any other circumstances he would have refused. As a consequence of the manner of his nomination, he was perfectly free in saying, when the matter was brought up, that he should, in case of election, follow consistently the path he has so clearly marked out, of opposition to the "ba-a-d man" idea and would give every such offender the extreme limit the law allowed. This remark was the direct cause of his defeat. One of the men who heard it, immediately spread it where it would do the candidate the most good or harm, depending on the light in which the matter is looked at. He then scratched all the tickets at hand, substituting the name of F. D. Foster for that of the regular nominee. The defeated candidate has no reason to be ashamed of the remark that caused his defeat and in that light his defeat is one of the highest compliments that could be paid them. Of course he does not relish the defeat itself, but he would far sooner be defeated than have it supposed that he would renounce the opinions he has always upheld. Frank D. Foster, the elected candidate knew nothing of the matter until after the election and freely expresses his opinion that it was a contemplible trick.
articles.summary: Explanation of A. T. Packard's defeat for justice of the peace: nominated at the urging of Willis Eaton and Gregor Lang, he vowed to punish 'bad men' to the limit, and someone scratched tickets to substitute F. D. Foster.
